paper_title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal search agents (Geng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2025; Narayan et al., 2025) answer information-seeking questions beyond static knowledge inside the model, such as identifying the source of the rare knowledge, cross-checking numerical claim against the live web, or assembling multi-step provenance argument across images and retrieved pages. Contemporary systems handle such tasks by orchestrating reasoning, perception, and live web search across many turns over fixed inventory of hand-crafted tools. It typically contains web search, webpage fetching, image grounding, OCR, depth estimation, and code execution. Throughout this paper, we use tool to Equal advising. Figure 1: We propose an automatic tool-generation framework for multimodal search agents. In the example shown, an agent restricted to fixed tool library is bound to its pre-defined primitives and fails on queries that no original tool can directly resolve. Our framework instead grows the library: the agent operates over an extended tool library that includes newly generated tools and can invoke them freely when solving real queries. Here, the newly generated Event In Image tool resolves the query through finer-grained information verification and image search. mean callable Python utility, exposed to the agent through typed schema, that takes structured input (a text query, an image, URL) and returns evidence the agents reasoning loop consumes in subsequent turn; generating new tool means producing new such callable schema, execution logic, and all, and admitting it to the catalog the agent draws from at inference. Nevertheless, hand-crafted tools suffer from inherent limitations. First, tool inventories shipped with production systems and developer-curated skill banks (VoltAgent and Contributors, 2026) are expensive to maintain and frozen at the developers anticipated coverage. When new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild, human intervention will be needed to modify the tools. Second, complementary lines of work that learn memory over fixed inventory (Xiao et al., 2025) or train an agent to use existing tools more efficiently (Gao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026) sharpen how the agent uses its tools but do not expand which tools it has. natural alternative is letting the agent itself generate the missing tool. Tool generation has been studied across adjacent domains such as vision language understanding, math and table QA, general NLP, and embodied / computer-use agents (Chen et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Wölflein et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023, 2025), but has not been carried over to multimodal search, where the inventory remains hand-authored. The transfer is non-trivial: search-agent trajectories are long, and agent state mixes images, link references, and tool outputs across turns. When exploring the world, human practitioners both use existing tools and fashion new ones when existing tools fall short (Goodall, 1964; Beck, 1980; Tomasello, 1999). We argue that multimodal search agent should be equipped with the same capability. When existing tools fall short, the agent should organically fashion new ones from familiar parts, refining and reusing them across tasks. Currently, multimodal search agents only share the using half of this picture but conspicuously not the fashioning half. When their tool set fails, they let it go rather than enlarge and revise the toolbox. Moreover, humans do not blindly adopt every novel implementation they sketch. They verify it on test cases before adding it to the working library (Schön, 1983). An agent equipped to grow its tools must also be equipped to verify them. To this end, we introduce TOOLSMITH, an automatic tool-generation framework organized as four model-agnostic phases: 1) Trajectory Mining, 2) Reuse-or-Grow Decision, 3) Tool Generation, 4) Two-Gate Verification. We cluster the agents failed trajectories into capability gaps (Shinn et al., 2023; Andrychowicz et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2025), check each gap against lean library of eight primitives to decide reuse versus generation, prompt generator VLM to author new tools as Python source under structural and anti-hardcode constraints, and admit candidates only after sandboxed sanity and LLM static code-review gates. We evaluate TOOLSMITH across 3 in-domain multimodal search benchmarks (FVQA, InfoSeek, EncyclopedicVQA) and 10 out-of-domain benchmarks under VLM-as-a-Judge manner. When using the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model, admitted tools improve the base tool library by +2.20pp indomain and +1.33pp out-of-domain tasks. Gains scale with backbone capacity, reaching +2.98pp out-of-domain on Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and consistent uplift on GPT-5. We also utilize comprehensive ablation study to demonstrate how different tool generation models and training samples affect the benchmark performance. Our code and data will be publicly available. Contributions. 1. We propose TOOLSMITH, to the best of our knowledge, the first automatic tool-generation framework for multimodal search agents, with model-agnostic four-phase pipeline over base tool library of search, visual, and codeexecution tools. 2. On 3 in-domain and 10 out-of-domain multimodal search benchmarks, admitted tools improve the base library across different models, with gains extending to larger backbones, which demonstrate the scalability and flexibility of our proposed TOOLSMITH. 3. We conduct ablation studies to analyze overhead, new-tool usage, tool-call distribution, toolfiltering, and failure modes, which provides an objective landscape of TOOLSMITH.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multimodal search agents. Our work targets multimodal search, where query is resolved by orchestrating reasoning, perception, and live web retrieval across many turns. growing collection of benchmarks frames this task: MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2025) couples multimodal query with curated search engine; MMSearch-Plus (Tao et al., 2026) adds provenance-aware verification; BrowseComp-VL (Geng et al., 2026) and MMBrowseComp (Li et al., 2025) raise cross-modal information-seeking difficulty; VisBrowse-Bench (Zhang et al., 2026b) targets visual-native search; and RealX-Bench (Hong et al., 2026a) couples finegrained perception with multi-hop retrieval. Beyond pure search, the landscape extends to embodied tasks that integrate web information with physical action (Hong et al., 2026b). These tasks build on vision-language understanding, where models must ground fine-grained visual evidence (You et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024) and abstain when the visual context is insufficient (Liu et al., 2024). Recent browsing agents tackle these benchmarks via hand-engineered tool inventories (Geng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2025; Narayan et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026), supervised finetuning or reinforcement learning that teaches tool use and action selection (Jiang et al., 2026a), or memory learned over fixed inventory (Xiao et al., 2025; Hasegawa et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026b). Our contribution is orthogonal: rather than freeze the inventory, we generate it. Tool generation. Building on lineage of LLMorchestrated modular vision-language reasoning (You et al., 2023), our work is closely related to recent line of methods in which the agent itself constructs new tools. GENOME (Chen et al., 2024) grows library of vision-module wrappers proposed by an LLM and validated on few-shot examples. CRAFT (Yuan et al., 2024) creates and retrieves Python tools for math, table QA, and image classification. TOOLMAKER (Wölflein et al., 2025) turns code repositories into LLM-callable utilities for general NLP. Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) grows an executable skill library for an openended Minecraft agent, with parallel line of work (Wang et al., 2025) carrying the idea to web agents via online programmatic skill induction. EvolveR (Wu et al.) distills past trajectories into textual principles that guide future behaviour, and WorldMind (Ren et al., 2026) builds symbolic worldknowledge repository from agent experience for physically-grounded action. Compared with these, we introduce the tool generation framework into the multimodal search domain.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: TOOLSMITH is organized as four-phase pipeline (Figure 2): Phase 1 mines capability gaps (query patterns the base tools cannot handle) from the baseline agents failed trajectories. Phase 2 decides, per gap, whether to reuse an existing tool or escalate to generation. Phase 3 prompts generator LLM to author the new tool as Python code. Phase 4 admits the candidate after verification gates. At inference time, lightweight retrieval step selects relevant generated tools per query. Notation. Let Aθ be the baseline agent, Dtrain the training pool, and Tt the tool catalog at round t, initialized with the eight base tools, T0 = Tbase. trajectory τ records the agents full tool-call sequence on single query. We write Gϕ for the generator LLM, ψ for sentence encoder, and cos(, ) for cosine similarity. 3.1 Phase 1: Trajectory Mining We roll out Aθ on Dtrain and apply two-layer trigger to each trajectory. Layer (cheap signal) flags any trajectory whose final answer the LLM judge marks as incorrect. Layer (LLM self-critique) then reads each flagged trajectory and assigns failure label from {NEW_TOOL_NEEDED, ARGUMENT_MISTAKE, SEARCH_NOISE, AMBIGUOUS}. Only NEW_TOOL_NEEDED trajectories yield capability gap, which we record as the tuple of (failing query, tools the agent already tried, the selfcritiques failure reason, and an image reference when image-grounded). Clustering. To ensure diversity in candidates, we embed each capability gap as the concatenation of its question, prediction, and gold answer using sentence encoder ψ, then apply agglomerative clustering (average linkage) over cosine distance into clusters. One representative per cluster enters Phases 24.

sections.title: 3.2 Phase 2: Reuse-or-Grow Decision
sections.content: Phase 2 decides, for each capability gap, whether the current tool catalog already covers it or new tool is needed. We compute the TFIDF cosine similarity between the gaps text (its query and subtask) and every existing tools description, and take the maximum: ρpre(g, Tt) = max tTt cos(cid:0)tfidf((cid:101)g), tfidf(dt)(cid:1), (1) where dt is the description of tool and (cid:101)g = qg sg If concatenates the gaps query and subtask. ρpre > τpre, the gap is treated as covered by the best-matching tool and skipped; otherwise it is forwarded to Phase 3. TFIDF suffices here because tool descriptions are short, the vocabulary is domain-specific (search, image, OCR, code), and we only need to detect obvious overlaps.

sections.title: 3.3 Phase 3: Tool Generation
sections.content: Phase 3 takes each gap that Phase 2 forwards and writes new tool for it. The output is candidate comprising Python source, typed schema, and short natural-language description, which is then forwarded to Phase 4 for verification. Representative code listings of admitted, failed, and filtered candidates appear in Appendix G.

sections.title: 3.4 Phase 4: Verification and Inference
sections.content: A candidate is admitted only if it passes both verification gates followed by redundancy check against the existing catalog. We run the gates in order of increasing computational cost: Gate 1 is cheap static check, so candidates that fail it are dropped before we pay for Gate 2s LLM critic. Gate 1: Sandboxed sanity. The candidates source is parsed and scanned for dynamicexecution and dangerous-I/O patterns, then executed once on minimal dummy input under tensecond wall-clock budget. Anything that violates the static checks or errors at runtime is rejected. Gate 2: LLM static code review. An LLM critic scores the candidate on four 05 axes (parametric usage, description abstractness, edge-case handling, and task alignment) and admits it only when the mean score is at least µmin and the minimum across axes is at least amin. The critic may use different model from the generator; tools with overly narrow descriptions or missing error handling are caught here. Feedback-driven retry. When either gate rejects candidate, we re-prompt Gϕ with short naturallanguage summary of which gate failed and why, up to per-candidate budget A. Empirically, most retries either pass on the second attempt or remain wrong for the same reason, so is capped at small constant. Tool catalog update. candidate that survives both gates is then compared against every existing tool by TFIDF cosine similarity over descriptions (the same construction as Eq. 1, with stricter threshold τpost). Only candidates whose closest match falls below τpost are admitted to the next-round catalog Tt+1; redundant duplicates are dropped. Inference. Exposing the full generated catalog alongside the base primitives would inflate the perturn schema and degrade tool selection. We instead retrieve per-query subset: each tool description dt is pre-embedded with ψ; given test query q, the agent sees Tq = Tbase top-K(cid:0)cos(ψ(q), ψ(dt)) ; Tnew (2) yielding Tbase + tools per sample. The base primitives are always visible (they are referenced by name in the agents system prompt); the generated tools rotate per query based on relevance. sections.title: 4.2 Tool-Generation Training Pool
sections.content: We collect trajectories from the train or val splits of three knowledge-intensive multimodal search 1https://serper.dev/ datasets: FVQA (Wu et al., 2025), InfoSeek (Chen et al., 2023), and EncyclopedicVQA (Mensink et al., 2023). The held-out test splits of the same three datasets serve as our in-domain (ID) evaluation in Section 4.3, providing within-distribution measure of whether the generated tools address the failure modes they were designed for. No example from any out-of-domain benchmark enters tool generation. We defer per-dataset sampling sizes and split choices to Appendix F.1. 4.3 Evaluation Benchmarks inWe evaluate TOOLSMITH along two axes: domain (ID) performance on the held-out test splits of the three datasets we used to mine capability gaps during training, and out-of-domain (OOD) transfer to ten public multimodal search benchmarks unseen during tool generation. Perbenchmark sample counts are summarized in Table 8, and full per-benchmark descriptions are deferred to Appendix B.1. In-domain (ID). ID evaluation uses the heldout test splits of FVQA (Wu et al., 2025), InfoSeek (Chen et al., 2023), and EncyclopedicVQA (Mensink et al., 2023). Because the training pool from which we mine capability gaps comes from the training splits of these same datasets, the test splits provide within-distribution measure of how well the generated tools address the failure modes they were designed for. We give full per-benchmark descriptions in Appendix B.1.1. Out-of-domain (OOD). OOD evaluation uses ten public multimodal information-seeking benchmarks: MM-BrowseComp (Li et al., 2025), SimpleVQA (Cheng et al., 2025), MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2025), MMSearch-Plus (Tao et al., 2026), HLE-VL (Phan et al., 2025), LiveVQA (Fu et al., 2026), BrowseComp-VL (Geng et al., 2026), RealX-Bench (Hong et al., 2026a), VDR-Bench (Huang et al., 2026), and VisBrowse-Bench (Zhang et al., 2026b). None of these share data with the training pool. For benchmarks that mix text-only and image-grounded items we restrict evaluation to the multimodal subset (queries carrying at least one image), so the reported counts are smaller than the full-benchmark totals. Appendix B.1.2 provides per-benchmark descriptions. Final-answer correctness is judged by VLM-asa-Judge prompted with GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), following (Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a); the prompt and discussion of retrieval-shortcut concerns are in Appendix B.2. 4.4 Models and Implementation Models. We consider three open-sourced models, including Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, and Qwen3-VL32B-Instruct, since all of them can cover different model sizes (8B vs 32B) and model variants (Instruct vs Thinking). For proprietory models, we consider GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07). We sample at temperature 0.3 with top-p 0.95, allow up to fifteen tool-calling iterations per query, and cap context at 120K tokens; full hyperparameters are in Appendix E. Evaluation protocol. Because the search APIs, the agents tool-routing decisions, and the LLM judge are all stochastic, every reported number is the mean of three independent runs.

sections.title: 5 Main Results
sections.content: Tables 2 and 3 report headline accuracy on the in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) benchmarks under three settings per inference backbone: Direct Inference (no tools), Agent Workflow w/ Base Tools (the eight-primitive base library), and Agent Workflow w/ Base and TOOLSMITH (GPT-5) (the base library plus tools admitted by TOOLSMITH when GPT-5 is fixed as the generator).2 The eight base primitives alone lift Qwen3-VL8B-Instruct by roughly +25pp on ID and +10pp on OOD over Direct Inference, with 32B and GPT5 showing comparably large jumps; multimodal search is clearly tool-driven task. Adding the TOOLSMITH-generated tools on top of the base library yields further consistent gains of one to three points on both ID and OOD across all three inference backbones, and the gains are pervasive per-benchmark: 32B and GPT-5 improve on every OOD benchmark and 8B improves on eight of the ten, with the remaining two essentially flat. The average gain peaks at 32B (+2.32pp across ID and OOD), with GPT-5 (+1.72pp) and 8B (+1.77pp) close behind for different reasons: GPT5s smaller gain partly reflects its privacy-refusal floor (Appendix B.4); 8Bs reflects the long-context tool-selection cost of an enlarged toolbox. sections.content: The inference-backbone axis is already covered by the main results (Section 5), which sweep Qwen3VL-8B-Instruct, 32B-Instruct, 8B-Thinking, and GPT-5 with fixed GPT-5 tool generator. This section ablates the remaining design choices: which model authors new tools, whose trajectories the pipeline mines, and how the cluster-count knob shapes the resulting tool bank. Because each ablation requires re-running Phases 14 of the pipeline end-to-end on the full training pool, we restrict every sweep below to one representative ID benchmark (FVQA) and one representative OOD benchmark (MMSearch) to keep the compute budget tractable.

The mid-range C=500 sits slightly above both C=250 and C=750 on the two benchmarks, indicating flat plateau rather than sharp optimum; we adopt 500 as the default and do not tune further.

sections.title: 7 Analysis
sections.content: 7.1 Overhead Both the one-time tool-generation cost and the perquery inference overhead of TOOLSMITH are manageable in practice. Due to space, we defer the full token, dollar, wall-clock, and per-query breakdown to Appendix H.

sections.title: 7.2 New-Tool Adoption
sections.content: Table 7 reports how often the agent invokes generated tools across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. On in-domain benchmarks, generated tools account for 27% of all tool calls, and 41% of samples invoke at least one, confirming that the agent actively selects generated tools when the query matches their capability. On out-of-domain benchmarks, adoption drops to 15% of calls and 16% of samples, which is expected since the tools were mined from in-domain failures. Nevertheless, the non-trivial OOD adoption indicates that some generated tools generalize beyond their training distribution.

sections.title: 7.3 Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: We examine the patterns behind gained and lost samples; four illustrated case studies appear in Figures 36 (Appendix I), and code-level tool examples in Appendix G. Why generated tools help. The dominant pattern is that generated tools enforce perceive-thenquery pipeline that the base agent skips. With only base primitives, the agent often jumps to text search without first identifying the visual entity. Generated tools chain reverse-image search with structured KB lookup in single call, forcing the correct order. For example, on What year did he give $50M to create the Hastings Initiative? (Figure 3), the base agent searches without identifying Reed Hastings and mis-attributes the donation to Eric Schmidt; the generated tool resolves the person first, after which single text search returns the correct year. change with time, exact numerical reproduction may drift. We pin model snapshots and archive trajectories to partially mitigate this, but building fully replicable environment for search agents remains worth pursuing in the future. Why generated tools hurt. Among the lost samples, failures concentrate on small number of tools that return incorrect information. Other losses stem from visual mis-identification or from the agent trusting generated tools output over correct result it had already obtained from base tool. Appendix walks through one successful tool, one runtime-failing tool, and one tool filtered out by Gate 2 in code-level detail. Adoption correlates with gain. The in-domain benchmarks, where adoption is highest (41%), show consistent accuracy improvements, while the lower-adoption OOD benchmarks show smaller or neutral changes, suggesting that the accuracy gains are driven by actual tool use rather than incidental prompt differences.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced TOOLSMITH, an automatic, modelagnostic tool-generation framework for multimodal search agents. Starting from an eight-primitive base tool library, it mines trajectories on training pool, generates new tools under our proposed TOOLSMITH framework. Across three in-domain and ten out-of-domain benchmarks, admitted tools improve on top of the base tool library on every benchmark, and gains persist across different inference models, and tool-generation models. Furthermore, we conduct more in-depth analysis on tool generation, tool use, and error samples. TOOLSMITH is step toward multimodal search agents that extend their own capabilities with minimal human curation.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: TOOLSMITH does not include tools that themselves generate images, such as those introduced by Gen-Searcher (Feng et al., 2026) and UnifyAgent (Chen et al., 2026b); we plan to leave the generative part, together with its safety controls (Zhang et al., 2026a), to future work. We have also not yet utilized code-specialized LLM as the tool-generator backbone, and we believe stronger code model would further improve the quality of admitted tools and downstream accuracy. sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: All datasets we use are publicly released for research and we do not redistribute them. Generated code runs in process-level sandbox with an AST allow-list and execution timeout, sufficient to block accidental misuse. We cannot control the commercial search APIs and proprietary models. But we have ensured that all of our uses are legal and appropriate. The potential risk comes from the external APIs, which may return harmful content. sections.title: LLM Judge Prompt
sections.content: You are an impartial judge evaluating whether deep research report contains the correct answer. [Question] {question} [Correct Answer] {correct_answer} [Deep Research Report] {response} Task: Determine if the deep research report contains the correct answer anywhere in its content. Instructions: 1. Read through the entire research report carefully 2. Look for the correct answer anywhere in the report (it may be embedded in paragraphs, tables, or sections) 3. Check if the information in the report is consistent with the correct answer 4. The answer does NOT need to be in specific format or labelled as final answer 5. Provide your reasoning 6. Answer with yes if the report contains the correct answer, no if it doesnt or contradicts it Output format: correct: [yes/no] reasoning: [your explanation] B.3 Performance Variance Text Search summarizer prompt (abridged) Because the agent issues live search calls and the randomness exists in LLM generation, repeated evaluations of the same configuration show run-torun variance. For the result numbers in Section 5, we report the average of three independent runs. B.4 Refusals on Identity Queries Some of our evaluation benchmarks contain queries that reference real person, such as who is the person in this photograph, what is the affiliation of this researcher. Proprietary models are increasingly trained to decline such queries under their privacy and identification policies, even when the gold answer is public-figure fact already widely indexed on the open web. We observe this from GPT-5 in our setting, which returns refusal in place of an answer, and the judge will count the refusal as incorrect. Therefore, in some of the benchmarks, the GPT-5 performance is lower than the Qwen3-VL-32B model or Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model.

sections.title: Webpage Visit extraction prompt
sections.content: Please process the following webpage content and user goal to extract relevant information: Webpage Content: {webpage_content} User Goal: {goal} Task Guidelines 1. Content scanning for rationale: locate the specific sections directly related to the users goal. 2. Key extraction for evidence: extract the most relevant information; preserve the full original context whenever possible. 3. Summary output: organize the result into concise paragraph with logical flow that connects the evidence back to the goal. Output: single JSON object with keys rational, evidence, and summary (each string; empty string if no content is available). No code fences, no Markdown, no extra keys. C.2 Visual Tools Zoom-in. Crop region of an image given normalized bounding box on the [0, 1000] scale plus padding, and return the cropped image. Used for closer visual inspection after the agent has already localized region of interest. Visual Grounding. Locate and highlight regions of an image that match text query, backed by SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026). It returns an annotated image with matched regions highlighted and numbered, along with bounding boxes. OCR. Extract readable text from an image, backed by PaddleOCR-VL (Cui et al., 2025). Returns the transcribed text as single string. Used when the task is about words, numbers, or printed labels in the image; not for general object localization or segmentation. Depth Estimation. Estimate per-pixel depth map for an input image, backed by Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025). Returns depth image (closer surfaces brighter, farther darker). Used when the task requires reasoning about relative distance, foregroundbackground separation, or 3D scene structure cues that flat 2D crops cannot resolve. C.3 Code-Execution Tool Code Execution. Run Python over the agents local computation state and the outputs of previously called tools (bounding boxes, OCR strings, segmentation masks, and so on), returning both standard output and the resulting local variables. The agent may pass snippet directly, or describe computation goal in plain language and let small coding LLM (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) author the snippet using prior tool outputs as named variables. Used for aggregating numbers extracted by OCR, filtering detected regions by bounding-box area, or any cross-tool numerical reasoning the agent cannot complete in its own response.

sections.title: D System Prompt
sections.content: Here is the system prompt of the agent. System Prompt You are visual reasoning agent that answers questions about images using structured Perception-Reasoning-Action framework. Your goal is to provide accurate, wellreasoned answers. You have access to various tools that compensate for known limitations of vision-language models. Use native tool-calling for tools. Do not write textual Action/Action Input to call tools. At most one native tool call is allowed per assistant message/turn. Use the following format: Question: the input question you must answer Observation: your direct perception of the input or the result of the action you took Thought: you should always think about what to do Action: the action to take, should be one of the provided tools, or Final Answer if you have final answer and do not need to call any more tools. Action Input: the input to the action, or the final answer if Action is Final Answer # Image-input rule: - Runtime image IDs are provided in Environment Update messages. - If tool needs image input, use those IDs in *_image_path fields. - Do NOT invent image file names or paths. # Tool-Use Rules - Call exactly ONE tool per turn. Never include multiple <tool_call> blocks. - Full tool schemas with parameters and types are provided in the <tools> section below. - After each tool call, verify whether the result is actually informative for the task. - If tool result is empty, missing key values, or non-informative, do NOT guess. Issue another tool call with corrected arguments or use different tool. # Available Tools You may call ONE tool per turn to assist with the user query. You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags: <tools> {tools_directory} </tools> For each function call, return json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags: <tool_call> {name: <function-name>, arguments: <args-json-object>} </tool_call>

sections.title: E More Implementation Details
sections.content: Model setup. For full reproducibility, all GPT-5 calls use the pinned snapshot gpt-5-2025-08-07 via the OpenAI API. All Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Qwen3-VL-8BThinking calls use the public Hugging Face weights served locally with vLLM. The LLM judge uses GPT-4o (Appendix B.2). Decoding. Temperature 0.3, top-p 0.95, repetition penalty 1.1, per-turn maximum 2,048 generated tokens, at most fifteen tool-calling iterations per query, and an agent context capped at 120K tokens. Pipeline hyperparameters. Phase 1 (Trajectory Mining). Sentence encoder ψ =BAAI/bge-m3 for embedding capability gaps; agglomerative clustering with average linkage over cosine distance; default cluster count = 500. Phase 2 (Reuse-orGrow). Pre-generation TFIDF reuse threshold τpre = 0.40. Phase 3 (Tool Generation). Percandidate retry budget = 2. Phase 4 (Verification). Gate 1 (sandboxed sanity) wall-clock budget 10 seconds; Gate 2 (LLM static code review) meanscore threshold µmin = 3.0, minimum-axis threshold amin = 1; post-gate TFIDF dedup threshold τpost = 0.55. Inference. Progressive-disclosure retrieval exposes the top-K = 10 generated tools per query alongside the base library.

sections.title: F More Tool Generation Details
sections.content: F.1 Training Samples Trajectories are mined from the result of the agent on three knowledge-intensive multimodal QA datasets, all distinct from the evaluation benchmarks (Appendix B.1). We sample 3312, 3000, and 2862 queries per dataset. Dataset FVQA (Wu et al., 2025) InfoSeek (Chen et al., 2023) EncyclopedicVQA (Mensink et al., 2023) Split (size) train (3312) val (3000) val (2862) Table 9: Tool-generation training samples and datasets. F.2 Generator Process Statistics We hold the inference model fixed at Qwen3-VL8B-Instruct and vary the model that authors new tools during Phase 3, running each on the same 300query FVQA training subset (search-required partition). Table 10 reports generation-process statistics; qualitative findings follow. Generator Trig. Succ. (%) Dedup Cost GPT-5 Qwen3-VL-32B Qwen3-VL-8B 73 83 83 50 (68%) 67 (81%) 24 (29%) 23 6 17 $1.03 $0.00 $0. Table 10: Tool-generator model ablation on 300 FVQA training queries. Trig.: queries whose self-critique labels capability gap. Succ.: candidates that pass both verification gates. Dedup: candidates skipped because near-duplicate already exists in the catalog. Local models incur zero API cost. GPT-5 produces structurally rich tools: modular helper functions, tiered authority ranking of knowledge sources, and multi-layer fallback chains. Qwen3-VL-32B passes 81% of candidates with clean but simpler code. Qwen3-VL-8B succeeds on only 29%; manual inspection reveals logic bugs that survive the gates but would fail at runtime (see Appendix for code examples). We adopt GPT-5 as the default generator, accepting its API cost in exchange for the structurally richer code. F.3 Tool Generation Prompts We list all prompts used in the tool-generation pipeline in execution order. 1. Self-critique (Phase 1, Layer B). Self-critique prompt (abridged) System: You are an analyst deciding whether failed multimodal agent run requires NEW tool to be invented. User: Question: {question} Final answer the agent gave: {prediction} Ground-truth answer: {gold} The agent invoked these tools: {tool_counts} Last tool errors: {recent_errors} Would NEW tool have let the agent answer correctly? Reply with one of: - NEW_TOOL_NEEDED: capability is missing - ARGUMENT_MISTAKE: right tool, wrong usage - SEARCH_NOISE: tools worked, bad results - AMBIGUOUS: question itself unanswerable If NEW_TOOL_NEEDED, describe: (a) input modality (text / image+text / image) (b) data source (website/API or web search) (c) which field of the gold answer to extract Reply: LABEL: <label> WHY: <one sentence> 2. Query classifier (Phase 3 pre-step). Classifier prompt (abridged) System: You classify question by its expected answer shape. Reply ONLY in 3-line format. User: Question: "{failed_query}" Reply with EXACTLY this format (3 lines): ANSWER_TYPE: <COUNTDATEBOOLEANENTITY_NAME FACTUAL_LOOKUPOTHER> ANSWER_LENGTH: <1-5_charsshort_phrase full_sentence> EXTRACTION_HINT: <what to extract from search> 3. Generator system prompt (Phase 3). Generator system prompt (abridged) You are Python tool author for multimodal deep-research agent. Write single new tool class that solves the failed query. The tool must: 1. Inherit from BaseTool 2. Call super().__init__() with: tool_name, tool_description, input_schema, ... 3. Implement execute(**kwargs) -> dictstrlist 4. Use only: requests, re, json, datetime 5. Chain-call base tools via HTTP POST to 127.0.0.1:8104/execute -- do NOT call external APIs directly 6. Take entities as parameters; do not hardcode Anti-hardcode rules: (a) No conditional-return lookup tables (b) No fake scores from string properties (c) No hardcoded reference constants 4. Seed examples (Phase 3, appended to system prompt). The system prompt includes six positive tool examples and one anti-pattern. Each example demonstrates different tool archetype: Seed example categories (code omitted) # Example 1: text-only KB chain # # (e.g. actress_by_character: query Wikipedia for an actress given character name) # Example 2: image-then-KB chain # # (e.g. fossil_identification: OCR image, then search KB for fossil species) # Example 3: narrow-domain HTML scrape # # (e.g. esports_player_stats: scrape specific game wiki for player stats) # Example 4: cross-modal lens+verify # (e.g. company_recognition: Lens to ID logo, # then verify via text search) # Example 5: structured-KB chain-call # # (e.g. entity_property_lookup: query Wikidata for specific property) # Example 6: vision zero-shot classification # # (e.g. best_label_by_image: CLIP similarity over label set) # ANTI-PATTERN (what NOT to write): # # # - Hardcoded lookup tables - Fake scores from string length - Specific entity in tool_description 5. Generator user prompt (Phase 3, per-gap). Generator user prompt (abridged) Failed subtask: query: {failed_query} Expected answer shape (from classifier): ENTITY_NAME answer_type: answer_length: short_phrase extract_hint: extract the person's name Image: {image_url} (Declare image_url in input_schema and chain-call vision tool) Failure reason: {self_critique_reason} Tools already tried: {tried_tools} Design single new tool that would have made this subtask succeed, then return the JSON. 6. Feedback retry prompt (Phase 3, on gate failure). Feedback retry prompt (abridged) You previously wrote tool for this subtask, but it did not pass the quality gate. Failed subtask: query: {failed_query} Quality gate feedback: {feedback} (e.g. "L1: tool chain-calls wikidata_query but never checks confidence field") Your previous code: ```python {previous_code} ``` Fix the issues flagged above. Keep what worked. Return the revised JSON. 7. LLM critic (Gate 2). Critic prompt (abridged) System: You are senior Python code reviewer. Score on FOUR axes (0-5 each). Return JSON: {parametric_usage, description_abstractness, edge_case_handling, task_alignment, critique} Axis definitions: - parametric_usage: Do declared parameters drive logic? Hardcoded returns score 0-1. - description_abstractness: Does description name CLASS of queries (4-5) or specific entity (0-1)? - edge_case_handling: Does execute() handle empty/None/invalid inputs gracefully? - task_alignment: Does the tool's purpose actually address the original failing query?

sections.title: G More Tool Examples
sections.content: We show more tool examples here, including successful and failed ones. Code is abridged for space. G.1 Successful Tool: Medical Condition Identifier Triggered by What skin condition is shown? The tool decomposes the problem into helper functions, ranks medical sources by authority, and chains five fallback stages. Key excerpts: Medical Condition Identifier (abridged) # Tiered medical-source authority ranking def _authority_score(self, domain): tiers = [ (100, ["wikipedia.org"]), (95, (90, (80, ["nih.gov", "cdc.gov", "who.int"]), ["dermnetnz.org", "mayoclinic.org"]), ["medscape.com", "webmd.com"]), ] for score, subs in tiers: if any(s in domain for in subs): return score return 30 def execute(self, **kwargs): # Stage 1: reverse-image search cands = self._pick_candidates_from_lens(matches) # Stage 2: fallback to Image Search if not cands: cands = self. _pick_candidates_from_image_search(...) # Stage 3: rank by authority score ranked = sorted(cands, key=lambda x: -x["score" ]) # Stage 4: extract from URL slug or title for in ranked[:5]: cond = self._slug_to_condition(c["link"]) if self._is_valid_condition(cond): return cond.lower() # Stage 5: last-resort -- visit the page directly _post("Webpage_Visit_Tool", { "urls": [best["link"]], "goal": "Extract the medical condition name" }) The tool embeds domain knowledge (medical authority tiers) and robust output normalization (15 word lowercase phrase, HTML/wiki markup stripped). The generated tool here also demonstrates the compositionality by composing base tools (Image Search, Text Search, and Webpage Visit) and then generate the new tool. The candidate below (with explanatory comments added) was triggered by single training query about named hurricane: Wrapper (abridged) Generator (codegen) Self-critique (trigger) Classifier (local 8B) 455 446 5.19M 2.77M $34.18 0.25M 0.70M $7.26 0.05M 0.02M $0.00 Total 5.49M 3.48M $41.44 Table 11: Tool-generation cost breakdown. Token counts are from the APIs reported usage field. GPT-5 pricing: $1.25 / 1M input, $10.00 / 1M output (reasoning tokens count as output). The classifier runs on local Qwen3-VL-8B at zero API cost. Wall-clock time: 170 minutes with 4 concurrent workers. At inference, the only added overhead is the perquery tool routing: single forward pass through sentence encoder (10 ms on CPU) followed by dot-product over the tool embedding matrix. sections.title: I Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: def __init__(self): super().__init__( tool_name="hurricane_wind_speed_lookup", ...) def execute(self, **kwargs): ... # Identify hurricane via Lens, then filter titles # by hardcoded name regex: if image_url: titles = [m.get("title","") for in matches[:5]] name_candidates = [t for in titles if re.search( r"b(hurricanestorm" r"erestoernesto)b", t, re.I)] ... The advertised scope is generic hurricane windspeed lookup, but the title filter hardcodes the literal target entity (ernesto) together with an autoregressive misspelling (eresto). On every other hurricane, the filter returns the empty list and the tool errors out.

sections.title: H Overhead Analysis
sections.content: Table 11 breaks down the one-time cost of running TOOLSMITH with GPT-5 as the generator at = 500, yielding 264 verified tools. The cost is dominated by completion tokens ($34.80 of $41.44 at the GPT-5 list price) because GPT-5s reasoning traces are charged as output. We present additional case studies; three patterns account for the gains: 1. Perceive-then-query. The generated tool chains visual identification (Lens) with structured lookup (Wikidata, text search), forcing the agent to identify the entity before searching for facts. The base agent often skips identification and searches for the wrong entity. 2. Specialized lookup. The generated tool directly answers specific attribute query (e.g. aircraft model year, building architect) via targeted chain-call pipeline, replacing the base agents generic multi-step search. 3. Forced verification. The generated tool prevents the agent from answering from internal knowledge alone (zero-tool hallucination) by requiring lookup step. Lost samples concentrate on few tools returning incorrect information, and on mis-identification where Lens returns similar wrong entity. Case studies. Figures 36 present four representative gained samples. The first three illustrate the perceive-then-query pattern at the entity (Figures 3 and 4) and region (Figure 5) levels; the fourth (Figure 6) shows generated tool re-ranking search results toward higher-authority sources even when both pipelines call similar primitives. Figure 3: Entity-first identification (Reed Hastings, $50M Hastings Initiative). The base agent searches without knowing who is in the image and misattributes the donation to Eric Schmidt; the generated Image Entity Canonical Name tool resolves the person first, after which single text search returns the correct year. Figure 5: Precise region identification on US map. Without explicit map-region parsing the base agent confuses Oregon with neighboring Washington and returns the wrong governor; the generated State Context Lookup tool pins down the highlighted state first, after which the governor lookup succeeds. Figure 4: Entity-first identification on person whose visual context provides only vague cues. The base agent guesses Mississippi from incidental visual content and returns the wrong pageant; the generated Celebrated Person From Image tool produces the canonical identity (Beatrice Luigi Gomez), which makes the event lookup trivial. Figure 6: Search-ranking steering. The base agents generic image search returns multiple election maps and the agent latches onto Reddit thread about the wrong year; the generated Event Name From Image tool primes the search for an event-name extraction and reorders the results so Wikipedia (1996) outranks Reddit (1968).
